scenes.text: Seven mornings, from fifteen hundred to twenty one hundred. In each one, you wake up as someone else, under the same Sun. The Sun won't change. You will. You start out going to bed when it sets. You end up in a world that might run on it. And at the end, you'll find out how old that light really is.

scenes.text: You wake up in fifteen hundred, in London. It's Midsummer Eve. You can smell wood smoke, and the streets are glowing with firelight. Did you know that almost everyone you'll ever meet believes the Sun goes around the Earth? That's what Ptolemy taught, about fourteen hundred years ago. So what is the Sun to you? Simple. It's the difference between day and night. Daylight is for work. Darkness is for sleep, and prayer. But tonight, nobody sleeps. Doors are hung with green birch and flowers. Glass lamps burn all night. Neighbours share bread and drink by the bonfires. Why? A London writer, John Stow, later wrote that a great fire could purge the infection of the air. Far away, a young Polish astronomer, Copernicus, is studying the sky. In fifteen forty three, the year he dies, his book puts the Sun at the centre. And within seventy years, a new instrument will show you something shocking. The Sun isn't perfect.

scenes.text: You wake up in sixteen ten, beside the River Thames. It's a cold, misty December morning, and the Sun hangs low and dim. A man named Thomas Harriot points a telescope straight at it. Don't try this. It can blind you. Did you know that the first telescope drawing of sunspots wasn't made by Galileo? It was this Englishman. And he never published it. Two years later, in Florence, Galileo watches the spots drift across the Sun, day after day. A rival says they're tiny planets passing in front. Galileo says no. They're on the Sun itself, and the Sun is turning. In sixteen thirteen, he publishes his letters. The perfect heavenly body has blemishes. Out in the fields, daylight still runs your day. But for a few people with telescopes, the Sun has become something to watch. Closely. And soon, someone will ask what's actually inside that light.

scenes.text: You wake up in seventeen seventy nine, in England. It's a bright summer morning, and the fashionable ladies outside are hiding from it, under parasols. Did you know that a pale face was so prized that fashionable women painted theirs with white lead? One famous beauty, Maria Gunning, Countess of Coventry, died at twenty seven. Her death was blamed, at least in part, on the lead in her face powder. If you're rich, you stay out of the Sun. If you're poor, you work in it, and your tan tells everyone. But this summer, the Sun is turning into something new. Something to explain. A Dutch doctor, Jan Ingenhousz, runs more than five hundred experiments on plants. He sinks leaves under water. scenes.text: You wake up in eighteen hundred, near Windsor. It's February. An astronomer, William Herschel, splits a sunbeam with a prism, and lays thermometers in the colours, their bulbs blackened. Did you know that the hottest spot wasn't in the rainbow at all? It was just past the red, where nothing was visible. He'd found infrared. Light you can't see. Now the Sun is something you measure, even where your eyes give up. Soon, gas lamps push back the night in London. In eighteen thirty nine, in Paris, a nineteen year old named Edmond Becquerel shines light on a cell, and it makes electricity. Tiny. But real. And in eighteen fifty nine, Richard Carrington sees a white flash on the Sun. Within a day, telegraph wires spark, and operators get shocks. The Sun can reach down and touch our machines. Turning that spark into power would take another century. But first, we'd find out what we'd been eating all along.

scenes.text: You wake up in nineteen twenty eight, on a crowded American beach. Hot sand. Salt air. And everyone's lying in the Sun, on purpose. Did you know that the famous story, that Coco Chanel started the suntan craze, is probably a myth? A historian traced it to an unsigned magazine article from nineteen seventy one. The real reason was work. Jobs moved indoors, so a tan stopped meaning the fields. It meant a day off. Now look in your picnic basket. Bread. An apple. The process that made them got its name in eighteen ninety three. Photosynthesis. Leaves catch sunlight and turn it into sugar, and nearly all life runs on that. Your lunch is stored sunlight. So, in a way, are you. The Sun used to be something to measure. Now, it's the source of every meal. Then, in nineteen fifty four, at Bell Laboratories, a silicon cell turns about six percent of sunlight into electricity. We'd learned that we live on sunlight. Next, we'd learn to harvest it.
